analysis.one_liner: Bars lawsuits against gun makers and sellers for harms caused when their guns are criminally misused.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 285-140 on April 9, 2003, but the Senate never voted, and Congress ended without it becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit any lawsuit — in state or federal court — seeking damages or other relief from gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, or their trade associations for harms caused by the criminal or unlawful misuse of a gun that worked as designed. It would also require courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuit already pending on the day it became law. A few narrow exceptions would remain, including cases of negligent entrustment, knowingly illegal sales, and design or manufacturing defects.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, and their trade associations gain protection from the wave of lawsuits that cities, counties, and private plaintiffs had filed against the industry over gun violence. The bill removes the industry's largest legal and financial exposure — the kind of litigation pressure that produced massive settlements in tobacco and lead paint — while leaving citizens' access to guns unchanged.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun makers, sellers, and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Bars any 'qualified civil liability action' — a suit against a gun or ammunition maker or seller, or a trade association, for damages or injunctive relief stemming from criminal or unlawful misuse of the product — from being brought in any federal or state court [S2, S5].
Requires courts to dismiss immediately any such lawsuit pending on the date of enactment, ending suits already filed by municipalities and private plaintiffs [S2, S5].

Preserves a small set of exceptions: suits over negligent entrustment (selling to someone the seller knew or should have known was a danger), knowingly willful violations of sale or marketing laws, breach of contract or warranty, design or manufacturing defects when the gun is used as intended, and transfers to someone convicted of knowingly supplying a gun for a violent crime [S3, S5].

analysis.who_pays: Shooting victims and their families, and the cities and counties that had sued the industry to recover the public costs of gun violence, would lose their ability to hold manufacturers and sellers accountable through the courts for the criminal misuse of guns. Ordinary taxpayers in those municipalities would keep bearing those costs without a legal avenue to shift them.

drawbacks.text: The bill grants the firearms industry a litigation shield no other consumer product industry enjoys: makers of cars, toys, or pharmaceuticals can all be sued when their products are misused or cause harm, but gun sellers could not be, leaving courts to dismiss pending cases immediately [S2, S5].

Litigation is one of the few tools that pressures sellers to adopt safer practices, such as responsible dealer conduct; eliminating that pressure removes a private, no-cost-to-taxpayers enforcement mechanism, which critics argued would leave communities to absorb the costs of gun violence [S2, S3].
The bill's stated findings declare the underlying lawsuits an 'abuse of the legal system' based on theories 'without foundation,' a one-sided account written into the statute itself [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core effect is a one-way transfer of legal risk away from a single industry and onto shooting victims and the municipalities that pay for gun violence. Supporters had a real argument — that holding lawful sellers liable for third-party criminal acts departs from centuries of product-liability law and could destabilize a lawful business. But the exceptions the bill leaves open are narrow, and the mechanism it uses — an outright federal prohibition plus immediate dismissal of pending cases — does not balance those concerns so much as end the litigation outright. It is industry protection legislation, drafted from the industry's findings.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 285-140, but after the Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee on April 10, 2003, no further action was ever taken, and the Congress ended with the bill still in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns (R-FL) introduced the bill on February 27, 2003, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S7].
The Judiciary Committee reported the bill as amended on a 21-11 vote on April 3, 2003, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S7].

A motion by Rep. Mel Watt (D-NC) to recommit the bill with instructions — a last chance to change or delay it before the final vote — failed 140-282, with every one of the 140 supporting votes coming from Democrats and none from Republicans [S7, S8].
The House passed the bill 285-140 on April 9, 2003: 221 of 228 Republicans voted yes, as did 63 of 205 Democrats [S7, S9].

The Senate received the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on April 10, 2003; the committee took no recorded action, and the bill died there when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry was better off for the time being, but the outcome was temporary: two years later, in the 109th Congress, a nearly identical Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act passed both chambers and was signed into law in October 2005, so the industry ultimately obtained the shield this bill died without. Shooting victims and municipalities that had filed suits ultimately lost their claims once the 2005 law was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, who won a near-identical law in 2005

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.role: Reported the bill to the House
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on April 3, 2003 and ordered the bill reported as amended on a 21-11 vote

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.what_they_did: Mounted a major campaign urging Congress and members to pass legal protection for gun makers and sellers

against.name: Rep. Mel Watt
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions; the motion failed 140-282

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on April 10, 2003, leaving it to die when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Passage split heavily by party — 221 of 228 Republicans for, 137 of 205 Democrats against — though 63 Democrats crossed over to pass it, and the Democratic motion to recommit drew zero Republican votes.

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and importers
industries.note: The bill bars damage and injunction suits over criminal misuse of guns that functioned as designed and dismisses pending cases, eliminating the industry's largest legal exposure. The industry's gain comes directly at the cost of victims' and cities' access to the courts.
Trade associations of gun makers and sellers — which themselves faced suits — are expressly protected from 'qualified civil liability actions' alongside their members.

industries.industry: Local governments pursuing gun-cost recovery suits
industries.note: Cities and counties had filed suits seeking to recover the public costs of gun violence; the bill would bar and dismiss those claims, leaving taxpayers to bear the costs.
The bill prohibits suits 'brought by any person,' eliminating a contingency-fee line of litigation that ran alongside victims' claims.
